His administration issued a 2022 Nuclear Posture Review that retained deterrence while limiting contemplated nuclear use to extreme circumstances and affirming risk-reduction commitments (E002, E003). It also cancelled the SLCM-N and B83-1 programs, actions that reduced some proposed capabilities, while pursuing continued triad and NC3 modernization (E016, E027). The unfavorable side is material: the administration did not adopt its earlier campaign position on no-first-use or sole-purpose policy, retaining possible nuclear use against some non-nuclear threats (E016, E017). Independent analysis also identified unresolved implementation risks from nuclear-conventional integration and absent detailed employment guidance (E018). GAO documented cybersecurity and governance gaps in nuclear-weapons and defense information systems, but those findings do not establish a Biden-directed operational failure (E025, E026, E040). The Democratic Republic of the Congo ratified the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in May 2022, a direct state-level restraint choice during his presidency (E024). Tshisekedi also requested completion of a cybercrime code, and his presidential cabinet validated a 2022-25 national cybersecurity strategy (E022, E029). Parliamentary consideration of a Digital Code and a CBRN program addressing chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear risks show movement toward governance architecture and capacity-building (E030, E032, E049). These are formal actions, not proof of implementation or effective control. The main adverse evidence is that OPCW material described only partial initial chemical-weapons legislation, while an IMF review found insufficient monitoring of banks' operational and information-technology risks and called for stronger cybersecurity supervision (E027, E031). No cited evidence shows nuclear possession, proliferation, nuclear coercion, near-use behavior, or realized catastrophe.
